note.p: Ab 1830 entwickelte Robert Hermann Schomburgk auf der Karibikinsel Tortola Pläne zu einer Forschungsreise durch Südamerika. Zuvor hatte er sich potenziellen Auftraggebern in Europa nur als Sammler von Pflanzen und anderen Naturobjekten angeboten. Nach und nach erweiterte er seine Interessen hin zur Erkundung der Geographie und Ethnographie der westlichen Guayana-Region (Rivière 2006, I, 5–9). In diese Zeit fällt Schomburgks Lektüre des Reiseberichts von Alexander von Humboldt in der englischen Übersetzung von Helen Maria Williams (Humboldt 1814–1829). Im Jahr 1833 fertigte Schomburgk eine Karte von Guayana, in die er sowohl Humboldts und Bonplands Orinokoreise aus dem Jahr 1800 als auch mögliche Routen einer eigenen „scientifick journey” eintrug (RGS-IBG Collections, Map Room, mr Venezuela S/S.2 ). Robert Hermann Schomburgk fertigte diese Karte nach eigenem Bekunden ohne Kenntnis von Detailkarten der Guayana-Region an. Gleichwohl weist sie eine deutliche Ähnlichkeit mit Humboldts „Carte générale de Colombia“ (Humboldt 1814–1834, Tafel 22) auf.

Schomburgk sandte seine Karte sowie den Hauptteil des Reiseplans („Remarks to accompany a Map [...]”, S. 1–56) am 7. Oktober 1833 aus Tortola an den Sekretär der Royal Geographical Society Alexander Maconochie. Wenige Seiten „ Remarks on the Rivers Orinoco, Essequebo and Branco [...] Continuation” (S. 56a–61) reichte er am 5. November nach (RGS-IBG Collections, Archive, CB 1/46). In seinem Plan schlug Schomburgk vor, die dreißig Jahre zuvor von Humboldt begonnenen geographischen Forschungen über das Bergland von Guayana und das Quellgebiet des Orinoko fortzusetzen. Die RGS entschloss sich erst ein Jahr später, Schomburgks Reise zu unterstützen. Sie erteilte ihm die Instruktion, 1) das Innere der Kolonie Britisch-Guayana zu erforschen sowie 2) Humboldts Ortsbestimmungen des Orinoko-Oberlaufs zu vervollständigen.

Sowohl Schomburgks Karte als auch der hier erstmals veröffentlichte Reiseplan basieren im Wesentlichen auf den Bänden 4 bis 6 der englischen Ausgabe von Humboldts Reisebericht. Darin beschreibt Humboldt seine Reisen auf den Flüssen Orinoko, Atabapo, Rio Negro und Casiquiare. Zudem enthalten sie geographische Forschungsergebnisse zum östlich der Reiseroute gelegenen Bergland von Guayana. Insbesondere ordnet Humboldt die kartographischen Mythen von El Dorado und dem in der Region lange angenommenen großen Inlandsee historisch ein. Außer der Williams-Übersetzung des Humboldt’schen Reisewerkes konsultierte Schomburgk die stark gekürzte und bearbeitete Übertragung durch William MacGillivray (MacGillivray/Humboldt 1832).

Schomburgk geht bei der Angabe und Umrechnung der Längenmaße in seiner geographischen Beschreibung nicht immer konsequent vor. Williams übernimmt in ihrer Übersetzung Humboldts Angaben von französischen toises. Schomburgk rechnet diese zumeist in das englische Tiefenmaß fathom um, behält aber bisweilen auch toises bei. Hingegen folgt er Williams bei der bloßen Übersetzung der von Humboldt in französischen lieues notierten Längen als englische leagues. Gleiches gilt für die Angaben in französischen pieds, die Williams (und Schomburgk ihr darin zumeist folgend) ebenfalls ohne Umrechnung der Werte in feet angibt. Eine Ausnahme bilden die Seiten 43 und 44, in denen Schomburgk ausdrücklich Toisen angibt und in englische Fuß umrechnet. Humboldts Angabe von milles übersetzen Williams und Schomburgk mit miles, was in beiden Fällen wohl der englischen bzw. statute mile entspricht.

div.p:
Amongst the expeditions, which since Columbus’
times have been undertaken to the new continent, shine
conspicuously von Humboldt’s Travels to the equinoctial
regions, the happy result of which has so vastly enriched
physical science, that those publications which issued
from Humboldt and Bonpland (his courageous
and elightened friend and fellow traveller) as the fruits
of their combined investigations during their perilious
journey, have been called by a competent judge a work
of gigantic extent and richness to which the modern
literature of Europe can hardly offer a parallel.Dieses Zitat entnahm Schomburgk dem Artikel zu Alexander von Humboldt im sechsten Band der Encyclopaedia Americana (Encyclopaedia Americana, VI, 470). Ein Großteil der Artikel dieses Lexikons basierten auf der 7. Auflage der bei F. A. Brockhaus erschienenen Allgemeinen deutschen Real-Encyclopädie. Weder in der deutschen Fassung (Real-Encyclopädie 1827, V, 431) noch in der englischen Übersetzung ist der Urheber des Zitats angegeben. – It
does not belong to my present subject to enumerate
the additions which science in general received
from this expedition, their value has been acknowledged
long before this by a grateful public and placed the
name of Humboldt amongst those, which even time
will not obliterate.

More than thirty years have elapsed since Humboldt
returned to Europe and his expressed wish, that he
soon might find a successor in a similar undertaking,
may have been partly realized, but still not to the full
extent as the philosopher wished. Several journeys
have been undertaken to Colombia and the Brazils, but
neither has had a pure scientific view for its object,
and though Geography and Statistics in general may
have reaped some additions by these casual journeys
Humboldt’s expressed hopes remain e
unrealized,–
no geographical situations have been determined,
no botanist has herbalized on the banks of the
Meta, Vichada, Branco and Negro.

The height of fame which Humboldt has reached
by his journey and his subsequent publications,
which resulted from the same, might perhaps pre
vent the planning of a similar expedition, where
the predecessor was so richly endowed with a genius,
which in his sphere stands single at the present
age, – but circumstances are the rulers of human
undertakings and though Humboldt determined
the nature of the Orinoco’s communication with
the Rio Negro, the more interesting object of their
journey, the mighty river’s sources, remained a
geographical problem. The hostile Indians prevented the travellers
from penetrating much further than Esmeralda. The
circumstances may have changed, and what Hum
boldt found at that time impossible, may be accomplished
by perseverance. But this is not the only stirring
impulse to action, the illustrious traveller expresses
frequently the wish, that several geographical positions
which unfavourable weather presented him to ascertain,
might be hereafter astronomically determined; – he
entertained likewise the hope, that a botanist might
herbalize on the banks of the rivers, Meta, Vichada,
Zama, Branco, Negro &c. &c. and says especially, that
a traveller, who was favoured with the hospitality of
the missionaries could spend a year on the bank
of the rivers Atabapo, Tuamini and Negro, and a
second year on the mountains of Esmeralda and
the upper Orinoco might easily triplicate the Species
described by Aublet and Richard.If a traveller, favoured like us by the hospitality of the missionaries, were to remain one year on the banks of the Atabapo, the Tuamini, and the Rio Negro, and another year in the mountains of Esmeralda and the Upper Oroonoko, he would no doubt triple the number of genera described by Aublet and Mr. Richard. Humboldt 1814–1829, 280–281. Vgl. Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 433. He was further
obliged to restrict his investigations only to the Skirts
of the Sierra Parime, and the interesting part, encompassed
by the branches of this mountain-chain, remained un
explored. Thus, a rich field has been left open for
further investigations, the happy result of which may
amply reward the dangers and perils connected with a
similar enterprise, and though but few in the lapse
of centuries could dare to enter the lists with a Humboldt,
whose rare talent possessed a variety of knowledge
to avail himself of every advantage, where opportunity
offered him to exercise the same, still I do not shrink
from planning a new expedition to South America.
Blessed with a strong constitution and acclimatized
during a sojourn of four years in the West Indies, the
most time of which was spent in botanical excursions
and surveying expeditions, accustomed therefore to
bodily exercise and possessed of some knowledge
of physics, I hope a European public will not
consider it presumptuous and chimerical at my
having resolved to undertake a scientific journey
to South America, provided I am encouraged and
assisted ; by and in this respect I have placed my
chief anchor of hope on England, which has always
shown herself ready to protect schemes of utility and
to give her powerful assistance to the execution of
plans, which have been connected with the advance
ment of science and the furtherance of useful know
ledge.

In order to become more acquainted with
the real object of my planned expedition, I attract
the readers’ attention to the following observations
which with the assistance of the annexed Maps will
partly point out my proposed route. The Map as well
as the observations have been mostly compiled from
Humboldt’s travels to the equinoctial Regions,
Bolingbroke’s Voyage to Demerary, Colombia 2 Vol. Volumes.
LondonWohl Walker 1822..
1822. – and for the further constructions of the map,
I have been assisted by "

and his map of the OrinocoNeben der großen Übersichtskarte „Carte générale de Colombia“, die den gesamten Lauf des Orinoko zeigt (Humboldt 1814–1834, Tafel 22), veröffentlichte Humboldt in seinem Physikalischen Atlas die „Carte itinéraire du Cours de l’Orénoque, de l’Atabapo, du Casiquiare et du Rio Negro“ (Humboldt 1814–1834, Tafel 16) sowie die Karte „Cours de l’Orénoque depuis l’embouchure du Rio Sinaruco jusqu'à l’Angostura. Dressé d’après des observations faites sur les lieux“ (Humboldt 1814–1834, Tafel 15). were unfortunately not
in my reach.

forms a triangle and extends from Latitude 12° .

It is connected with the northern part of the new

mountains which extend along the western coast,
and stretch from north to South, or from Cape

This mountain-chain, which is famed for its

div.p:
This singular division of mountains ,
forms three
great basins, which contain ⅘th of the whole surface
of South America; between the mountains of
Venezuela and the groupe of Parime extend the
plains of Apure and the lower Orinoco; between
the Sierra of Parime and those of Brazil’s are the
plains of the Rivers Amazon, Negro and Madeira,
and between the mountains of Brazils or the
Chiquitos and the southern end of the continent
are the plains of the Rio Plata. These division
distinguishes divisions distinguish the valleys of the three great rivers,
which drain the whole continent, the Orinoco,
the Amazon, and the Plata.

The llanos and plateaus or elevated plains, are
striking features in the Geography of South America.
The llanos, the first of which extends i. e. that is, from the mountains of Caraccas ,
to the forests of Guiana and the delta
of the Orinoco. over a space of 250,000 sq. square miles
and forms three divisions connected by narrow
openings, two of which, namely the llanos of
the lower Orinoco and those of the Rio Plata or
Buenos Ayres, are overgrown with grasses; the one
which is situated between them, or the llanos of the
river Amazon, is covered with impenetrable wood. The
plateaus or tableland of the Andes are inferior in extent,
scarcely 100 .
miles in circuit, but they are from 8 .
to
9000 feet elevated above the seathe plains of quito are 12,000 feet above the level of the sea. and are separated by
deep valleys.

The climate of this vast continent is colder than
other regions under a similar latitude. Many of the
summits of its mountains are covered with perpetual
snow and even under the line, the heat is not found so
extreme, as one would suppose; arising very probably from
the narrowness of the country and the elevation of the
land. In some of the countries on the banks of the Amazon
and the Rio Negro it rains during ten months of the year
and there are other places on the shore of that continent
where none falls for several years. But generally speaking
two seasons divide the year, the dry and the rainy.

No one can imagine the clearness of the atmosphere
between the 4th and 10th degree of northern Latitude
from the month of January to that of December; the sky
is then constantly cloudless,Nothing can equal the clearness of the atmosphere from the month of December to that of February. The sky is then constantly without clouds [...]. Humboldt 1814–1829, IV, 404. Vgl. Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 204. the llanos, these immense
plains which in the rainy season display a beautiful
verdure, are scorched, and assume the aspect of a desert;
the earth cracks and whirlwinds raise large clouds
of dust; the alligators and the large serpents remain
buried in the dried mud, till they are awackened awakened from
their lethargy by the first showers, which set in ;
at
the Orinoco about the end of April.The Llanos and the Pampas of South America are real steppes. They display a beautiful verdure in the rainy season, but in the time of great drought assume the aspect of a desert. The grass is then reduced to powder; the earth cracks; the alligator and the great serpent remain buried in the dried mud, till awakened from their long lethargy by the first showers of spring. Humboldt 1814–1829, IV, 297. Vgl. Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 149. The heat increases
progressively, the azure colour of the sky disappears
and a grey tint is spread over it; dense vapours
cover the atmosphere, which is conovulsed by frequent
thunderstorms; the rain falls in torrents, and the rivers rising
above their banks, innundate the surrounding plains. Thus
the woody marshes of Guiana are rendered insalubrious and
become the abode of swarms and insects, which are the unceasing
torment of men and beasts.

In these climates nature is marked by the most
stupendous features and its scenery abounds in the sublime
and beautiful; thus are its productions as peculiar as
its features and the wonders which it exhibits are but
sparingly known in European countries. Since Hum
holdt and Bonpland’s return, we have alone become
acquainted with 87 .
Species of Palm trees, these
characteristic und distinguishing signs of tropical
vegetation, the pride of warmer climates, which alone
give grandeur to a landscape by their lofty forms and
majestic appearance. The banks of the Orinoco and
Amazon are clothed with forests of the greatest
extent, characterised by a variety, and a
magnificence to which the graphic and discerning
pen of a Humboldt could only do justice. Enormous
plains extend their verdant surfaces beyond the
visible horizon and the most juicy fruits, and aromatic
trees, which diffuse a delightful odour, arrive to a
perfection which no other region can boast of.
The cultivated ground yields the sugar cane, the
coffee-tree, the Cocoa, the latter of which grows wild
in some parts, as well as cinnamon, vanilla,
the nutmeg, pepper, the camphor tree, the delicious
Ananas, Oranges and a variety of other fruits;
many medicinal plants and various sorts
of woods, used for dyes and carpentry. The Cow-
tree is peculiar to South America, being famed for
the abundance for of glutinous and nutritious
milk which its trunk yields, when incisions are made
in the same, and European grain is likewise
cultivated upon fields, which rise from 5 to 9000 feet
above the level of the sea, which gives to South America
the advantages of the torrid and the temperate zone.

In Guiana the air is filled with numerous
butterflies of the most splendid colours and in the
forests, myriads of shining flies astonish the
traveller by night. But as if to counterbalance these
shining peculiarities of the torrid zone, insects
exist, which occasion the greatest annoyance to its
inhabitants. Thus are the different tribes of tipulae
of which the mosquito forms a species, – and of
the tribes of reptiles, the largest and most venomous
snakes, e. g. for example the boa constrictor, the rattle snake and
several other kinds, dangerous for their being armed
with deadly poison. The rivers abound in fishes and
likewise in Alligators. A variety of birds, distinguished
by the richness of their plumage or their size, from
the Colibri to the condor, people the trees of the
forests and the plains. Apes of the most fantastic appearance
are distributed through the woods – t . T he peculiar
tribe of quadrupeds, defective with respect to teeth,
appear to be confined to the new world, thus
are the sloth, the ant-eater, the Armadillo. The forests
are neither void of beasts of prey, and the Jaguar
and Puma or Couguar (Felix(Felis) onca and Felis
concolor & discolor, commit depredations and the
first attacks even men. Extensive plains are
covered with herds of horses, mules and oxen, the offspring
of European racesThese animals were introduced by the spaniards in 1548.
and have since multiplied to that extent, that
Humboldt supposes millions to rove wild over the
llanos during the period e
of his travels, the export
from Venezuela to the West India Islands amounted annually to
30.000 mules
147,000 cow-hides
and 140,000 Arobes of Tassajó or slightly salted
and dried meat.
. Nor is the mineral kingdom poor
in productions; Brazil produces diamonds, gold; and
other parts of South America abound in iron, tin, lead,
quicksilver – like precious ores are found in Chiles and
the silver-mines of Potosi are famed for their risk returns.

This vast empire was formerly almost in the sole
possession of two European nations, the Spaniards and
Portuguese, but with the exception of Guiana, it is at
present entirely independent of Europe. It is divided
into the empire of Brazil, the Republics of Colombia,
Venezuela, Peru, Eucador Ecuador , Bolivia, Chile, Buenos Ay
res or the united Provinces of la Plata, the Banda
oriental, Paraguay and the terra del Fuego, the latter of which
is in the possession of the natives; the whole population
having been estimated at between 13 .
and 14 .
million, there
would not be more than 2 .
persons on each square
mile of its superficial area. The inhabitants are composed
of whites, Indians and Negroes and their mixed races.
The whites are mostly creoles, the number of Europeans
is but small. The Indians or native tribes are in some
parts still independent, and have been in others subdued
and mostly converted to the catholic religion. The Negroes
are Africans or descendants of Africans.

When I spoke of the groupes of mountains, which
subdivide the southern part of the new Continent,
I mentioned likewise the Sierra Parime, and after having
given a rapid sketch of South America in general,
I shall now dwell more particularly on the country
encompassed by this chain and its branches, as it is
to form that region, to the investigation of which, I
intend to dedicate the first years of my planned expe
dition. But I shall prefer to point out firstly the
main object of my journey, and to propose a route
which shall conduct me to the s a ttainment of the same
and like the traveller, whose steps lead him gradually
to new prospects and to the beauties of a favoured
climate, describe on the way the prominent features,
which according to those, which visitted visited or described
these regions before, astonish the wanderer or attract
his contemplative and reflecting mind to the mighty handiwork
of the creative power.

The object of this planned journey is
1. to examine the features of the country, its
mountains, – the bed and banks of rivers, whether
navigable, whether tributary streams or the
confluence of several – the river’s descent, the
productions of the soil, through which it
drains, the country’s climate – its animal
and vegetable Kingdom.
2. t T he Character of the inhabitants – whether
civilization has been attempted or is in
progress and by what nation, or what
prospects there are for attempting it; –
furthermore to make most minute
observations, whether trade might be carried
on with them, in what the barter probably
would consist and in what way the same
might be carried on to the greatest advantage
for Europeans.
3. To determine geographically the country, which
I investigate, by ascertaining astronomically
the most prominent features and to collect such
materials, as will assist in forming accurate
delineations of the same and to neglect no
opportunity to note such phaenomena
as might contribute to a description of its
physical Geography.
4. To form not only collections of plants, but
likewise of minerals, insects &c. &c.

Conformable to an expressed wish of the Royal Geogra
phical Society of London, I would commence my
researches in Demerara, and laying the investigation
of the Imataka mountains (between the 7th and 8th
degree of northern latitude) for the present aside, I place
the reader at once on the river Essequebo, which is
nine miles west from the Demerary River, and its
mouth abo ut ve
twenty miles wide. At the mouth of
the same are three Islands, which are valuable for
the high state of their cultivation; the easternmost
is Leguan, that in the centre Walkenaam and the
next Tiger Island, which form four entrances into
the river. Southward of these are a succession of
other Islands, which extend five and twenty to
thirty miles beyond the first. About fifteen miles
from the mouth is Fort-Island, which was formerly
fortified, but is now in decay. The tides of the
Essequebo are pretty regular and extend nearly a
hundred miles up. The confluence of the rivers Coyoni
or Cuyuni and Mazerony, with the Essequebo takes place
about forty miles belowabove the rivers river’s mouth ( Lat. Latitude 6° 24′ north).
The Rinocote and the Usupama mountains give an

from Arinda (a former military post Lat. Latitude 5° 30′ N. North )
to the mouth of the Rupunuri. Long before we approach
the confluence of these three rivers – (where there was former
ly opposite the stream Tupuro a Dutch military post, Kyk-over-al) all traces of
cultivation have disappeared, and the eye observes only
an impenetrable forest, which stretches from both
sides of the river deep in the interior. The next river
of consequence which flows into the Essequebo, is the
Sibarona, the sources of which are found on the
northern side of the Pacarayna mountains, at
the same time the Tavaricuri, a tributary stream
of the Rupunuri originates on the southern side
of the same groupe of mountains – thus drains
the Essequebo both declivities.

The Rupunuri falls at 4° 10′ Lat. Latitude into the Esse
quebo; between one of its tributary streams, which
I named already, the Tavaricuri and the stream
Pirara, a tributary of the Mahu, exists a land

two rivers and over which the boats are either carried
upon the shoulders of the crew or dragged upon collers –
I shall henceforth call them “Portage” (Portage), – a second one is more southerly
between the Rupunuri and the Sarauri, which flows
into the Tacutu. The first European which crossed
the latter portage was Nicolas Hortsmann a native from
Hildesheim in Germany and who had settled as surgeon
in Guiana. Attracted by the reports of great riches which
might be discovered in the interior, he manned in
1739 .
a canoe (coreal) with Indians, and ascended the
Essequebo and followed its course by dragging the
canoe along its rapids and causing it to be carried
across the narrow neck of land, until he reached the
Rio Branco, which he descended to the Rio Negro
and arrived in 1740 in Pará. Here he met the french
academician M. Condamine, to whom he communi
cated a map of his route and a sketch of his journal
This was very likely the journal, which afterwards was

At a later periode (1793) Don Fr. José Rodriguez

and but lately there arrived (February 1811 .
) several

Having crossed the more northern portage
between the Tavaricuri and the canno Pirara, we

high mountains, which since the 16th century
encircled the Laguna de Parime or the lake of

period are but imperfectly known and which

which inhabit Demerara, to which I shall refer the
readers for information.

It was my intention to speak before this of the
different groupes of mountains, which we have
passed in our route, but as particular interest
is attached to the spot which we have reached
and which obliges us to make a halt and to
recall by-gone days; I shall repair this omission
and give now a connected view of the most distinguished
branches of the whole System which Humboldt has
called the System of Parime.Humboldt 1814–1829, VI, Part II, 503; Humboldt 1814–1825, III, 220 (Le système des montagnes de la Parime).

list.item:
I. The base of the mountain-barrier, which separates
the plains of the lower Orinocco Orinoco from those of the Rio
Negro, extends from the 3d to the 8th parallel of N. Northern
Latde Latitude
and between the 66th and 68th Meridian (counted west
from Greenwhich). Its general direction is westward which
course is likewise kept by its lateral branches; – from
the mouth of the Apure to the delta of the Orinoco,
the distance of the ridge from the banks of the river
is generally 10 .
to 14 .
miles; some detached groupes
approach however its very banks and form the rapids
of Tomo Torno , the Boca del Infierno and the narrow
passage at St. Saint Thomas, from which the town has
been named Angostura.

A 1 . The most northern branch of this groupe, is the
one which extends from the Río Arui (7° 50′
All the parallels are northern and the Meridians
west from Greenwhich, where the contrary is not
observed. ) to
Angostura and from thence towards the Rio Carony and
the sources of the Imataca (62°
merid. meridian )

1 2 . Another groupe rises from the basin of the Rio
Caura, where they form the rapids of Mura; they
stretch to the springs of the Río Cuchivero and encom
pass by a detached branch Encaramada.

2 3 . The next are the Chaviripe mountains (7° 10′), which
send off a branch to the southward (– 6 .
° 20′ to 6° 40′ –)
and being connected with the Corozal and Amoco
mountains, this groupe joins lastly the high ridge
of the Matacuna mountains.

4. The Baraguán forms the narrow passage of the
Orinoco (7° 5′) which has received its name from
this mountain-chain (Angostura del Baraguán).
It takes afterwards its direction ,
towards the mountains,
which separate the sources of the Rio Caure from those
of the Ventuari.

5. At latitude 6° 25′ rise the Carichana mountains,
of wild appearance but interspersed with rich pasture
grounds.

6. The western bank of the Orinoco, which ha ve s been
mostly level, distinguishes itself by the Peak of Uniana,
which rises from a plain to the height of above more
than 3000 feet (6° 42′) – the dyke which forms
the Cataract of Apures ,
diverges from the Peak of Uniana
and rises on the eastern shore to a groupe, which
approaches the Cerro Cunero (5° 35′ to 5° 40′ .) ).

7. The larger Cataract of the Orinoco is formed in
the vicinity of Maypures by the Quittuna mountains,
distinguished by the Peaks of Catalimini, Cunavani.

8. The last branch of this range are the Sipapo mountains
4° 50′) which at the distance of some miles from the
Orinoco, rise on its eastern bank, and which compose
the S. South
W. West ridge of this system. β. It may be propable probable
however that a western branch extends to the sources
of the rivers Uraupes and Negro, the highest summits
of which, reach scarcely 800 feet. γ. The eastern branch
of this groupe, composed of the mountains of the
upper Orinoco and to the eastward of the Raudal
de Guaharibos (1° 15′ merid. meridian 65° 18′) are entirely
unexplored. They are connected with

II. the Sierra Pacarayna (Pacaraymo, Pacarahina)
They were already known by these names after Raleigh’s
return from Guiana.
the main ridge of which is but small, though they
extend from the river Anocapra ( Longt. Longitude 63° 15′) to
the left bank of the river Rupunuri ( Longt. Longitude 59° 30′) a
distance of 260 .
miles. On the northern foot of the
Pacarayna mountains are the sources of the Rio
Anocapra; the Araicuque and the Uraricapara which
derive their sources from the southern declivity, are
subjected to overflowings and form in the vicinity
of the demolished mission of Santa Rosa (3° 46′ –
Longt. Longitude 62° 59′ –) the valley of inundation (El valle
de la Inundación). Detached groupes of this chain
form the mountains of

1. Tauyana, where the Rio Parimé has its
sources.
2. the Crystal mountains (3° 36′ Longt. Longitude 60° 32′)
3. the Marcarapan, with elevations of 3000 feet.

On approaching the banks of the Essequebo, the
mountains run in a more South eastern direction
and stretch to 2° 30′ northern latitude. We distinguish
in this groupe

4. the Cumucumu mountains
and further eastward derives the Rupunuri or Rupu
nirini its sources from the
5. Vassari mountains

β On the right bank of the Rio Branco, in a still
more southern direction (between the 1st and 2d parallel)
is a mountaineous country, in which the rivers
Caritamini, Padaviri, Pacimoni, originate. The western
branch divides the basin of the Upper Orinoco from that of
the Rio Negro and joins the mountains of Unturan
and Yumariquin, which run off in a south eastern
course from Esmeralda.

γ :
We are much less acquainted with the develop
ment of the mounitains-range between the 59th and
64th
parallel meridian , or between the Sierra Pacarayna and
the river Coyoni. Don Antonio Santos and D. Nicolas
Rodriguez left Angostura in 1775 .
and ascended the Carony
to the mouth of the Paraguá (7° 8′) which they then
followed to the river Paraguamusi and entered lastly
the Anocapra (or Nacoprai), where they crossed the
Sierra Pacaryna to Santa Rosa, from whence they
descended the Urariapara and arrived in San Joaquin.
This is the only line of route which has been pursued
by whites and upon their remarks rests our knowledge.

S. More easterly, under the 6th parallel are the mou
mountains of Usupania and Rinocotte, with the latter of which
we are already acquainted, as affording by a break a passage
to the Mazarony; and branches of the first form the
rapids in the Essequebo. All real knowledge with
respect to the continuation of that chain, S. South
E. East from
the Essequebo, is a desideratum. The interior of
dutch, french und portuguese Guiana, is according
to Humboldt a terra incognita.The geographer, who would ground a map of South America on observations of latitude and longitude, finds on the north of the Amazon a terra incognita three times as big as Spain. (Humboldt 1814–1829, V, 788–789, Anm. ♰).Le géographe, qui veut appuyer une carte de l’Amérique méridionale sur des observations de latitude et de longitude, trouve, au nord de l’Amazone, une terra incognita trois fois plus grande que l’Espagne. (Humboldt 1814-1825, II, 682–683, Anm. 3).

III. To the eastward of the Vassari mountains (2° 25′ Longt. Longitude
59° 30′) which are a branch of the Sierra Pacarayna,
runs a mountain-chain, which the missionaries
call Acaray and Tumucuraque It appeared firstly on the map of La Cruz.. These mountains,
which may be traced from Esmeralda (3° 19′) till
near the Cape North (1° 50′) separate under the second
parallel the northern sources of the Essequebo, Maroni
and Oyapok, from the southern of the Trombetas,
Curupatuba and Paru; they approach the banks
of the Amazon within a distance of 50 .
miles.

div.p:
Thus I have extracted from the more detailed
observations of Humboldt, a cursory account of
the Sierra Parima, which is ninetimes nine times larger than
Switzerland and extends, independent of the groupe of
mountains near the sources of the Rio Negro, from
Maypures to Oyapok, over a space of more than 1180 .
miles (69½ .
m. miles to a degree); their greatest breadth from the
mountains of Imataca to the sources of the Rio
Paru (a tributary stream to the Amazon) amounts
to 490 miles.

Connected with the Sierra Parima, is the El Dorado,
a fabulous country, where Gold and precious stones were said
to be as common as rocks in other counties. Lais Luis Daça, a
a famous Conquistador, received the first information
in Quito from an Indian, who told him and the assembled
Spaniards, of the immense riches, which were to be found
in his country, where the gold was so plentiful, that
a great prince used to cover his body with gold-dust.
A letter from Oviedo to Cardinal Bembo mentions, that
Pizarro, after he had discovered the province of the cianna
mon trees, went in search of a great prince, who
used to cover his body in such a way with gold-dust
that his resemblance from head to foot was a una
figura d’or a o lavorata di mano d’un buonissimo orifice.
It has been thought that Orellana received the first informa
tion of the gilded man El rey ò hombre dorado, which was abbreviated in El Dorado on the Amazon river in 1540.Vgl. dazu und zum Folgenden: Humboldt 1814–1829, V, 814; Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 694–695.
but so early as 1536 .
Gonzalo Diaz was in search of the
Dorado, and it was not till 1540 .
that Francisco
Orellano Orellana , disappointed in his expectation of finding
El Dorado in the Provincia de los Canelos, descended
the great Amazon.

Reports placed El Dorado at a later period on the
banks of the Paraguá (near the imaginary lake of Cassipa)
and afterwards between the sources of the Essequebo and
Rio Branco. Antonio de Berrio commissioned
Domingo de Vera, his Maese de Campo, to spread the
report of the immense riches which were contained
in El Dorado, which was henceforth called Manoa or
Laguna de la gran Manoa. He invited adventurers
to engage in an expedition, which had for its
object the conquest of this fabulous country. Rich
men sold their properties in order to engage in this
crusade, which consisted of 2000 .
men and had in
its train 12 .
Franciscan monks and 10 .
other clergy
men. The number of men which took part in
this expedition encreased during their stay in Cumaná and
Trinidad – from whence they embarked for the Orinoco
(1596 .
); however sickness, want of provisions, and
the hostile disposition of the natives, prevented them
from ascending higher than the Paraguá, and out
of the number which formed the expedition, only
thirty returned in a miserable condition to Santo
Thomé.

Raleigh who planned his expedition to Guiana
in order to recover the favour of Queen Elisabeth,
gave her an account of the riches which contained
„the golden and imperial city“ and of that „gilded king“
whose chamberlains furnished with long „sarbatanes“
blew gold-dust every morning over his body, having
first anointed it with aromatic oils.Vgl. dazu und zum Folgenden Humboldt 1814–1829, V, 390; Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 486. It is obvious
that Raleigh himself believed on in this fabulous country,
which he knew only from reports. He constructed
a map of the same, which he sent to Lord Charles
Howard, with the request to keep it secret; in spite
of which precaution, the Geographer J. Hondius published
in 1599 a description of Guiana, accompanied by
a map, on which the imperial city of Manoa
figured.

The little success which accompanied Raleigh’s
four expeditions to the lower Orinoccoo and to
El Dorado lessened the zeal of adventurers; Nicolas
Hortsmann, who we already know, thinking to find
El Dorado in the interior of Guiana, ascended the
Essequebo and arrived on the lake Amucu, where he
found that twhat had been taken for gold, was only mica
and the precious stones, Crystals.

During the time that Don Manuel Centurion was
Governor of Angostura, an Indian named Arimuicapi
arrived there, who told the Spanish Colonists fabulous
accounts of riches and attracting their attention to
the magellanic clouds, he told them that it was the
reflection of a solid rock of silver, which was placed in the
middle of the lake Parime; which induced Don Manuel
to send Nicolas Rodriguez and Antonio Santos in 1775 .
in search of this lake See S. page 17.

The isthmus which extends between the Rupunuri
and Branco, was by J. Hondius transformed on his
map of Guiana (1599) into the lake Rupunuwini or
Dorado; the length of which is 200 .
leagues, its breadth
40 .
leagues extending between 1 .
° 45 .
′ southern to 2 .
°
northern latitude. Later charts placed the same more
easterly, and its western end was to the south of the
delta of the Orinoco. Compare the maps of Blaeuw 1636 . ,
Sanson 1656 and
1669. M. d’Anville adopted the
Laguna de Parime in the second edition of his map
of S. South America (1760) and connected with the same the
rivers Orinoco, Branco and Essequebo by the Mazarony
and Coyoni. He placed the lake Parime
between the
third and fourth parallel, where formerly the
lake Cassipa was situated.

La Cruz Olmedilla (1775 .
) followed the example
of d’Anville. He places the sources of the Orinoco
under the name of Parima or Puruma in a mountain
ous country, between those of the Ventuari and Caura, at
the 5th parallel of latitude, where they rise from a
small lake Ipava. After having continued its course
40 .
leagues in a an east-north-eastern direction and 60 .
leagues
in a south-eastern and received the waters of the mahuMahu,
the river empties itself into the lake Parime, the
length of which is 30 leagues, its breadth 20 .
leagues; this
lake gives origin to the rivers Ucamu, Idapa, and
Branco – the Orinoco or Parimé disappears under ground
on the western foot of the Sierra Mey and emerges at
the 2d parallel, 3½° to the East of the meridian of
Esmeralda. The new river runs 50 .
leagues in a
west-north-western direction, when the it receives the
waters of the Ucamu and afterwards those of the
Rio Maquiritari, which arises between the lake
Ipava and the lake Cavija.

The rivers which are situated in the vicinity of
the Sierra Pacarayna, namely the Urariapara, Parimé,
Xurumu &c. &c. are subjected to overflowings. The right
bank of the Urariapara is known by the name of the
valley of inundation. These overflowings and the existence
of a small lake Amicu or Amoca, in the vicinity of
the Rupunuri, may have given rise to the imaginary
lake of Parime, which figured till lately upon the
maps of South America. The lake Amucu is upon Arrowsmith’s maps transformed
in into a village, which has been faithfully copied by Tanner
(South America with improvements to 1823. by H. Henry
S. Schenck Tanner), Phila
delphia) in his American Atlas, i on whose map the
Orinoco derives its origin from the lake Ipava and continues
its course to Esmeralda as represented on the adjoined
map by a green dotted line. On the same maps of Tanner’s
figure likewise the lake Cavija and the river Maquiritari.

The existence of the Amucu has already been asserted by Horts
mann and confirmed by later travels. I have chosen for my
route, the Portage which exists between the Tavariacuru and
the Canno Pirara – it will give me an opportunity to determine
that lake and the junction of the Tacutu and Urariquera. The
fabulous accounts of the El Dorado and the lake Parime have
likewise assisted to influence me, to prefer the northern
isthmus for the southern.

Arrived at the Portugeese Portuguese fort of San Joaquin, I purpose
to remain there for some time, if circumstances will permit
me to do so. Humboldt in his directions for a future expe
dition towards the sources of the Orinocco, points out par
ticularly this place, from whence the same might be
undertaken. There is no doubt that I might receive here
the necessary information, whether it would be praticable
to penetrate from there towards the sources, or whether Esmeral
da was more preferable for this purpose. This is not the
only circumstance which makes a prolonged stay in
San Joaquin desirable; – no botanist herbalized as yet on
the Sierra Pacarayna, and with the exception of the maps
of the Rio Branco, which were executed by Pontes Leme
and Almeida de Serra (1787 .
and 1804 .
) the rest of this
region is still a terra incognita. Being then in the
vicinity of Santa Rosa and the Rio Nocaprai, an
excursion thither would tend to encrease geographical
knowledge.

If I should not succed to penetrate from San
Joaquin to the sources of the Orinoco, it is my intention
to descend the Rio Branco to its junction with the
Rio Negro, which river I would follow upwards to the
mouth of the Padaviri.

We have seen that a branch of the montains of
Parime stretches southward, of which the Cerro Unturán
is one of its highest summits.See S. page 17 This small groupe of
mountains is rich on vegetable productions, distinguished
by the creeper from which the curare poison The Mavacure of the natives is prepared,
the Juvias (the fruit of the Bertholletia excelsa, our Brazil
nut of the shops) the aromatic berries Puchery (Laurus
Pichurim) the wild cacao, the Sassaparilla (Smilax
Siphilitica) &c. &c. The tributary streams of the Orinoco
are separated by this range from those of the Cassiquiare,
and Rio Negro. The northern, or the tributaries of
the Orinoco are the Mavaca and the Daracapo, the
western or those of the Cassiquiare, the Idapa and
Pacimoni, and the southern of the Rio Negro, the
Padaviri and Cababuri. The latter has a western
divergent at no great distance from its sources, which
has been named Baria and which communicates
with the Pacimoni; the other branch takes its course
in a different direction and flows in the vicinity of
Nstra Nossa
Shra Senhora
dos das Caldas into the Rio Negro. This ramifica
tion affords therefore the strange instance, that the
river which originates on the eastern declivity of the
mountain range at some distance offrom its sources
branches off and flaws in opposite directions; the
main branch takes its course easterly and the Baria
or the western branch sends in succession its waters to the Pacimoni,
the Cassiquiare and Rio Negro; thus after having
made a circuitous route of 110 leagues, we may
say that the waters which were joined at its sources,
and branched off, unite again where the Cababuri
joins the Rio Negro. The Cababuri has likewise a
communication with the Rio Dimity. The Portugueese Portguese
have availed themselves of its ramifications to penetrate
towards the lake Mavacca, which is northerly situated
from the Cerro Unturan, in order to collect the Sassaparilla
and the aromatic berry Puchery.

Though it might be connected with less difficulty to
reach Esmeralda by the Cababuri, in consequence of its
communication with the Mavaca being well known
to the Portugueese Portuguese Indians, I should prefer to ascend the
Padaviri, whose sources, I am led to suppose, can not cannot be
far northward from the Cerro Unturan and offer very
likely a portage with the Mavaca. The Padaviri has
never been explored; the tribes dwelling on its banks
are perhaps acquainted with the Orinoco and its sources.
After having reached the Mavaca and having its
situation and that of the lake and the Cerro Unturan
astronomically determined, a few days journey would
bring me to Esmeralda, the most solitary and remote
christian settlement on the upper OrinocoHumboldt 1814–1829, V, Part II, 502; Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 541., which
during the time of Humboldt’s visit contained 80 .
inhabitants
who appeared to live in complete poverty, their misery
being greatly augmented by the perpetual torments from
swarms of insects.

Esmeralda is celebrated for manufacturing the
curare-poison. It is extracted from a liana or creeper
called bijuco bejuco de Mavacure, a plant which Humboldt
supposes belongs to the Strychnos family. It is employed
by the Indians as an active and deadly poison (in which
they dip the points of their arrows) used in war and
in the chase, and strange to say, likewise as a remedy
for gastric obstructions. The Ticuna poison from the
Amazon, the Upas tieute from Java, the Curare of
Guiana, are the most deadly substances of vegetable poison
and yet the same may be tasted (and the latter is used as
a stomatic) without danger, for like the venom of the
snakes, it only acts when introduced into the vascular
system.

The peak Duida, at the foot of which Esmeralda
is situated, appears to be one of the highest summits
of the Sierra Parime; its elevation above the plain of
Esmeralda is 7155 .
feet and above the level of the sea
8400 feet. Its summit is so steep that no person
has ever ascended it. The granites of Duida contain
in open veins, fine rock crystals, some of them
of great transparency, which were taken for
diamonds and emeralds, in consequence of which
the village received the name „Esmeralda“. This
delusion has long since vanished and the miserable
village is now regarded as a place of banishment for monks .
and loaded with their malediction. – At the commence
ment and at the end of the rainy season, small flames
which remain not on the same spot, have been ob
served on the summit of the Duida; on this account,
the mountain has been considered volcanic, which
is however not the case. A similar phaenomenon
is to be observed on the top of the Guaraco, opposite
of the mouth of the river Tamatama. As already
oberved, the Duida is composed of granite, which
is full of drusy cavities, some of which are open,
others are filled with crystals and common earthy
sulphur; it is therefore probable that gaseous and
inflammable vapours pass through their fissures.

Humboldt dwells upon the picturesque scenery of
Esmeralda; – the groupe of the Duida rises in an amphi
theatre on the right bank of the Orinoco, surrounded by
a lovely plain, trenched by rills of black but limpid
water and decorated by groves of the Mauritia palm,
which is the Sago-tree of America. At the foot of the
mountains, where the marshy ground becomes a
savanah, large pine-apples are found of a delicious
flavour, growing solitary among the grasses, like
our meadow- siaffron saffron (Colchicum autumnale), while
the karatas, an other species of the Bromelia is a social
plant, like our heaths and whortles. They assist
to embellish the verdure around the Duida, their yellow
fruits crowned with a tuff of silvery leaves, rise above
the Paspalum and other Cyperaceae.

The site of the mission, continues Humboldt, is
highly romantic, the surrounding country is lovely
and of great fertility.Vgl. zum Folgenden Humboldt 1814–1829, V, part II, 511. Helen Maria Williams übersetzt allerdings das französische Original (La position de la mission est infiniment pittoresque, Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 545) wörtlich mit: The site of the mission is highly picturesque. I never saw clusters of plantains of so
large a size as here, and indigo, sugar and cacao, might
be produced in abundance, if any pains were taken for their
cultivation. The Savanah around the Duida affords
pasture and if the Franciscans of the College of Píritu,
possessed only a part of the activity of the Catalonian
Capuchins, who are settled on the bank of the Carony,
numerous herds would graze between the banks of the
Cunucunumo and the Padamo; – under present cir
cumstances not a cow, not a horse, is to be found.

To the east of the Duida, which on its north
western side is connected with the Cuneva and Sipapo
mountains, extends the Sierra Maraguaca. On the
left bank of the Orinoco, between the rivers Amaguaca and
Gehette are the mountains of Yumariquin. The Raudal
of Guaharibos is about 6½ days journey from Esmeralda.
In two days, one reaches the mouth of the Padamo, where
the Orinoco is from 3 .
to 400 .
fathoms in width. The
tributary streams from the right bank are more
numerous than those from the left, because the river
drains the Sierra Maraguaca, which collects the clouds.
The richness of the vegetable Kingdom, is on the northern
shore surprising; Humboldt mentions as an instance
the trunk of silk cotton tree (Bombax ceiba)
which was 16 .
feet in diameter. The missionaries of
the upper Orinoco were formerly in communication ,
with those of the river Caura by means of the Padamo.

From the mouth of the Padamo, which is of
considerable width; the Indians arrive in one day
and a half at the mouth of the Mavaca, between
both rivers the Ocamo falls on the northern
bank into the Orinoco. The Matacona, a tributary
to the Ocamo, arises where the Guainares Indians
are living; they differ from the other Indians
in having a less coppry skin and belong
to those tribes, which the missionaries call
Indios blancos.

In the vicinity of the mouth of the Ocamo
is a remarkable granite-rock; it is very likely a Gneiss
passing into granite and which is remarkable
by the ramification of its veins and its crystallization;
the Spaniards call it Piedra Mapaya (map-rock).
The distance from the mouth of the Mavaca
to that of the Río Gehette amounts to two
days journey. The Orinoco has diminished in
depth and width and the canoe must from time
to time be dragged over land. On the southern side
is the Daracapo and the Amaguaca which en
compass the mountains of Guanaya and
Yumariquin, where the Juvias, the fruit of
the Bertholletia are collected; on the northern
side is the Río Manaviche, which arises at the
Cerro Maraguaca. The more one advances, the
more difficult becomes the ascent of the river;
in consequence of its numerous windings
and many rapids, which obstruct the way. One
passes to the left the Canno Chiguire on the sources of
which an other tribe of white Indians, the Guaicas are
living. At the distance of two leagues from the latter stream,
is the Raudal de Guaharibos; a dyke of granitic rocks
fills here the river; these, says Humboldt, are the pillars
of Hercules, which no white person has crossed as yet.[...] these rocks are the columns of Hercules, beyond which no white man has been able to penetrate. (Humboldt 1814–1829, V, 560).[...] ce sont les colonnes d’Hercule au-delà desquelles aucun homme blanc n’a pu pénétrer. (Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 569)
Don Francisco Bovadilla, Commander at the Fort
San Carlos, having understood that several fugitives
Negroes from dutch Guiana had passed the narrow
ton gue of land, which divides the basin of the Cayoni
from that of the Orinoco, and had joined the inde
pendent Indians; he undertook an expedition without
the Governor’s permission, in order to surprize them
and to use them for his services. Bovadilla arrived
without obstacles at the lower rapids opposite the
Rio Gehette, – but having advanced to the Raudal of
Guaharibos and being with his parthy party at breakfast,
he was surprized by the Guaharibos and Guaycas
Indians, who not being acquainted with firearms
and seeing that the Spaniards had neither bows or
arrows, they found themselves encouraged to attack
unarmed men and wounded several of Bovadilla’s
parthy party , who saw himself obliged to fire upon them and
to kill a great many. The rest fled and the Spaniards
did not consider it prudent to advance further.

The Guaharibos blancos have constructed a bridge
of lianas across the Orinoco, somewhat above the
cataract, which is fastened to the rocks. This bridge
with the existence of which the inhabitants of Esmeralda
are well acquainted, proves that the Orinoco must have
been very small on this place. The Indians say that
the same is only from two to three hundred feet wide
and to be no more a river but only a mountain
stream (viachuelo). The Indians have a post at the
Raudal de Guaharibos, armed with bow and arrow,
to prevent every white person, or every person coming
from the abodes of the whites, to penetrate further to
the eastward. This prevented Humboldt from advancing
further than the small river Guaupe, from whence
it is still 15 .
leagues to the Raudal.

For a future discovery of the sources of the
Orinoco, Humboldt advices, that a small detachement
of soldiers should be sent out from Angostura or
Rio Negro and as he is persuaded, that the number of
these hostile tribes has been greatly exaggerated, he thinks
that they will be able to show sufficient resistance,
in case they should be attacked.Vgl. Humboldt 1814–1829, V, Part II, 575 sowie Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 577. Though he points
out three routes, namely from Esmeralda to the
eastward, by tracing the river to its sources – or by
the southward, by taking advantage of the Rio
Carony and Paraguá – or to the westward by the Rio
Branco and Urariquera, .
the first route would be
the most favourable. It is not likely that the upper
Orinoco, which is known to the Indians by the name
of Paraguá (sewhich signifies water, great water, sea) is
called by either of these names at its sources; the result
would remain therefore doubtful, if the expedition had
been undertaken from the south- or west-ward, unless
the discovered sources had been identified by following
their course to the mouth of the Rio Gehette.

Humboldt supposes that the sources of the Orinoco
are in Lat. Latitude 3° 40′ N. North – Longt. Longitude 63° 50′ W. West ; the mission
of Santa Rosa being, according to the portugueese Portuguese
maps in Lat. Latitude 3° 45′ – Longt. Longitude 63° –′, the distance
from thence to the sources could not be more than
60 to 80 .
miles. I observed previously that I would
try to procure myself every information on this
head in San Joaquin, and if my endeavours there
should not be crowned with success, then Esmeralda
shall be the place from which I intend to penetrate
towards the sources. Humboldt visi tt t ed Esmeralda at
the very commencement of the present century – more than
a generation have has since past passed away and the change of
circumstances may have produced likewise a change
with respect to the character of these hostile tribes. They
might be gained over by small presents and oppose
no further, what could not be considered an
encroachment upon their rights.

The Orinoco is not mentioned by this name upon the
celebrated maps of Diego Ribero, which was published in 1529.
Diego de Ordaz sailed for that river in 1531 .
and was nominated
Adelantado of all that land, which he might conquer between
Brazil and Venezuela, then called the land of the German Society
of the Welser ’s s .Bartholmew Welser of Augsburg, a privy counsellor of Charles
V., equipped in 1528 .
three vessels in Spain, which sailed
under the command of Ambrose Dalfinger of Ulm to
America, where he took possession of the province of Venezuela.
The emperor gave this province to Welser as a pledge for
1.200.000 florins, which he in company with the family
of the Fugger ’s s had advanced to him. They remained twenty
six years in possession of Venezuela, but after the death of
Charles V. the Spaniards deprived them of it. (Belzares). He sailed along the banks of the
lower Orinoco, but suffering shipwreck, returned with the
crew in two small boats to the mouth of the Amazon, where
he fitted out a second expedition. It was during this voyage
that the name of the Orinoco was heard for the first time;
Ordaz reported that the stream from its mouth to the
Río Meta was called Uriaparia, and above the Meta
OrinucuThe upper Orinoco or Paraguá, is called by the Maquiritares
Indians ,
Maraguaca in consequence of the mountain
range, through which the river flows above Esmeralda. which word is derived from the language of the
Tamanaks.

In longtitude longitude 66° 17′ W. West and latitude 3° 10′ north – five
leagues below Esmeralda, is the celebrated bifurcation of the
Orinoco. The stream flows from its source through the mountains
of Maraguaca and Guanaja; as soon as it reaches the opening
of the valley or the depression of the ground which terminates
only at the basin of the Rio Negro, it divides in two branches
the principal branch or Orinoco continues its course west
north-west and turns round the groupe of the mountains of
Parime, while the other arm flows off south-ward and
joins the Rio Negro. It appears consequently, that the two
first rivers of South-America, the Amazon and the Orinoco
have strictly spoken, only one basin. The upper Orinoco
and the Amazon pursue their course through the
same plain, with this difference; that the first flows from
east to west, while the latter on the contrary runs from
west to east. On a surface of 204000 .
square leagues and as
far north as the sources of the Rio Temi (in 2° 45 .
N. North )
all streams are tributaries to the Amazon; but further
north, by a remarkable formation of the country, an
other hydraulic system occurs, wh th at upon a surface
of scarcely 1500 sq. square leagues is drained by the Orinoco,
the sources of which are thus situated, that one
would think they belonged to the basin of the Amazon.
The branch which flows off south-ward, after the
division of the river has taken place, is known by
the name of the Cassiquiare. The existence of this
strange bifurcation remained long a problem, like
the course and termination of the Nigre Niger . Sir Walter
Raleigh appears to have been entirely unacquainted with
the communication of the two rivers. The Jesuits Christoval
de Acunna and Andrés de Artedia Artieda received the first
information, when in 1639 .
they travelled in the
suite of Captain Texeyra from Quito to Gran-Pará.
The Indians told them that the Rio Negro (which in
consequence of its dark waters was called Curiguacura
or Urana) gave an arm to the Rio Grande, that empties
itself into the northern ocean and the mouth of
which was surrounded by dutch settlements.Los primeros Indios que pueblan un brazo que el Rio Negro
aroja por, donde segun informacion se viene salir al
Rio Grande, en cuya boca en el mar del Norte estan
los Olandeses, son los Guaranaquazanas, Acunna, p. page 32Acuña 1641.
by Humboldt Vol. Volume IV. C. Chapter 23.Humboldt 1814–1829, IV, 477.) Not being
acquainted with a river of that name, Acunna concluded
that this could not be the Orinoco, but the Rio Felipe.
The connection of the two rivers remained doubtful until M.
de la Condamine, during his first voyage to the Amazon
in 174
6.1743 .
received new proofs of its existence through an Indian
woman from the Cauriacuni nation, who arrived at
Gran-Pará in a Canoe from the missions of Pararuma
on the lower Orinoco. Before M. de la Condamine returned
to France, the communication was placed beyond doubt
by the journey of father Manuel Roman and the casual
meeting of some missionaries from the Orinoco and the
Amazon.

Since the middle of the seventeenth century, the
Portugeese Portuguese undertook expeditions to the Spanish provinces,
in order to procure themselves slaves from the Indians in
exchange for glass-beads, hatchets, fishing apparatus &c.
These slaves were individuals of other tribes, who had
been made their prisoners during war, carried on for that
purpose. The Portugeese Portuguese entered the Cassiquiare, where it joins
the Rio Negro and following its course, they arrived at a
great river, with the name of which they were unacquainted.
In order to give to this these expeditions the appearance of some
justice, missionaries accompanied it, who decided whether
the seller had any right to the slave (poitos). This un
lawful j traffic reached such a height, that the Spanish
missionaries became alarmed, and father Roman, the
superior of the missions on the upper Orinoco, resolved to under
take a journey to the Guipunaves (the most cruel and the
most warlike tribe) in order to induce them to discontinue
their predatory practices. Unaccompained by any Spanish
Soldiers, he left Carichana on the 4th February 1744; as he
arrived at the confluence of the Rios Guaviare, Atabapo and
Orinoco, he discovered at some distance a canoe of the same
size as his own, filled with persons apparently dressed
like Europeans. As a signal of peace and according to
the usage of missionaries, when travelling through a
country unknown to them, he ordered the cross to be fixed
on the prow of the canoe. The others, in the strange
canoe (it were Portugeese Portuguese slave-dealers from the Rio
Negro) recognised under loud acclamations the garb of
the Order of St. Ignatius, and they heard to their greatest
astonishment, that the river on which they met, was
the Orinoco. They returned with father Roman to the
Portugeese Portuguese settlements on the Rio Negro, where he
was obliged to remain for some time. On his return
he chose the same route by the Cassiquiare and the
Orinoco, and after an absence of seven months, he
arrived on the 15th October 1744 .
at Pararuma. –
During the expeditions to the boundaries in 1756 .
,
under the command of Ituricaga and Solano, the
connection of the two rivers was ascertained in
a more detailed manner, and since that period e
there passed annually several boats from Angostura to
the Rio Negro; – nevertheless M. Buache published in
1798 .
a „Carte générale de la Guyane“, where he
denies this communication and calls it a geographical
absurdity. Humboldt’s researches proved its existence
most satisfactorily, and he was the first who determined
it astronomically.

The Cassiquiare flows at the commencement south
west; – „its banks“, says HumboldtHumboldt 1814–1829, V, 441. Vgl. Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 511., „offer no longer a beach
– a pallissade of tufted trees forms the bank of the river,
appearing like a Canal of more than 1200 feet in width,
bordered by two enormous walls, clothed with leaves and
foliage.“ – The Itivini, a divergent of the Cassiquiare,
branches off in about 2° 30′ northern latitude and forms
a similar communication between the Cassiquiare
and Rio Negro, as there existss between the Orinoco and
the Rio Negro by the Cassiquiare. It discharges itself
under the name of the Rio Conorichite, a little above
the mission of Davipe into the Rio Negro, where it
appears to be 120 .
fathoms in width. This river is
notorious for the traffic of slaves, which the Portugeese Portuguese
formerly carried on upon the same, and by which they
entered the Spanish provinces. They ascended the
Cassiquiare, entered by the Canno Méé ,
the Conorichite
and from thence arrived, partly by a Portage ; , on the
river Atabapo. The expedition of Solano in 1756 .
and
the foundation of Spanish settlements on the Rio
Negro, stopt stopped this revolting trade.

Pursuing the course of the Cassiquiare, we
come next to the mission of Vasiva, situated on an
island, surrounded by a lake of about a league in
width, which communicates with the river. The
water of this river lake is black, while that of the river
Idapa is white; the latter, like wise a tributary to
the Cassiquiare, descends from the Cerro Unturán and
offers at its sources a Portage with the Mavacca.

The Pacimoni discharges itself into the Cassiquiare a little
below the mission of Mandavaca, and though its sources are
at no great distance from those of the Idapa, its waters
are never the less nevertheless black. The Pacimoni belongs to that
system of rivers from which the inhabitants say, that they
possess black waters „aguas negras“. The colour is supposed
to arise from a mixture of carbon and hydrogenHumboldt 1814–1829, V, 191. Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 389. . and the The
Indians attribute it to the roots of the Sarsaparilla
which grows in large quantities along the shores of
several. When seen in a large body, they appear brown
or of a greenish black but when the least breath agitates
their surface, they become of a fine grass-green, not unlike
to the lakes of Switzerland; yet they are beautiful clear
and limpid, so that they reflect the images and colours
of surrounding objects and the smallest fishes are visible at
the depth of twenty or thirty feet. The Zama, Atabapo,
Matáveni, Tuamini, Temi, Rio Negro &c. belong to
the same system. As the lake of Vasiva and the Pacimoni
have black waters, it is a strange phenomenon, that
the Idapa which flows between them should be white.
The Pacimoni offers an other instance of a remarkable
ramification; the Baria diverges at no great
distance from the sources of the former river Cababuri
and flows into the Pacimoni , as I related already at another
place.

The rock of Culimacari has become celebrated from
Humboldt’s having determined on that place, the geographical
situation of the mouth of the Cassiquiare; it is situated in
2° 0′ 42″ northern latitude and probably in 67° 13′ western
longtitude longitude and Humboldt deduces from this these observations,
that the mouth of the Cassiquiare is in latitude 2 .
° 2 .
′
north and in longtitude longitude 67° 39′ 45″ west. These observations
are the more of importance to Geography, as several errors
existed in that respect in previous maps.

San Francisco de
Solano is the last mission on the
Brazzo Cassiquiare; it received its name from one of the
Commanders of the expedition to the boundaries, Don Joseph
Solano, and was not founded by monastic but by military
authority, like the most of the missions to the south of the
great Cataracts. The state of the christian settlements on
the river is described by Humboldt as being so deplorable,
that on the whole extent of its course, about fifty leagues,
there are not to be found three hundred inhabitants and
the number of canoes, which at that time annually passed
the Cassiquiare, were scarcely five.

p.ref:
From the mouth of the Cassiquiare it is about eight
miles to the Fort San Carlos del Rio Negro and as in the
vicinity with the junction of that river, it turns suddenly
from east to south-west, the rock of Uinumana affords an
opportunity of seeing from there, this majestic arm of the
Orinoco in its whole width. The Cassiquiare ressembles
very much the Rio Negro, with this difference, that it possesses
white waters and that near the rapids of Uinumana
it appears to be wider. Its width till above Vasiva ,
may
amount from about 270 .
to 300 fathoms.
p.note: Vgl. Humboldt 1814–1829, V, 401 und Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 491–492.

div.p:
It was thought that the engineer Don Gabriel Clavero
had erected the fort San Carlos exactly under the Equator,
but this is not the case; later Geographers have been aware of
his mis-statement, however they have differed in its real
situation until Humboldt determined to same to be
in parallel 1° 53′ 42″ north. The Equator traverses the
Rio Negro, according to his surmise, between San Felipe
and the mouth of the Rio Guape. The situation of the sources
of the Rio Negro is still dubious; according to the Statement
of Indians, they are a four or five days journey from the mouth
of the Pimichin, which induces Humboldt to believe that
they are in longtitude longitude 69° 16′ west. The confluence of the
Rio Negro and the Amazon occurs under the 60th meridian
near Barra de Rio Negro, where it is according to M. de la
Condamine upwards of 12 ,
00. Toises (= 7680 feet) across.

On returning from our diversion and following the
course of the Orinoco, we pass the junction of the rivers
Cunncunumo, Guanami, Purunama, whose banks appear
to be entirely deserted by human beings. Rude figures re
presenting the sun, the moon and different animals, which
are to be seen on the granitic rocks, attest the former existence
of people, which appear to have been more civilised, than
those which inhabit at present the banks of the Orinoco.
– Descending the river, we pass the mouth of the river
Jao and may reach the mission of Santa Bárbara
in thirty-five hours, after we have left Esmeralda. It is
situated near the confluence of the Ventuari, which next
to the Guaviare is perhaps the largest tributary stream
of the Orinoco. It forms at its junction with the Orinoco ,
a delta, girted by palms; at a distance of two days
journey it is joined by the the Cumaruita and somewhat higher up by the
Parú, both of which descend from the high mountains
of Cuneva. The Rio Manipiare, an other tributary,
comes from the west, but that part of the Rio Ventuari
which is above the mouth of the river Asisi, is almost
unknown. There are several Portages between the
sources of its tributary streams ,
and the rivers
Caura and Carony. It appears that the Caribs formerly
ascended the Rio Carony, entered the Paraguá and arrived at
the sources of the Paruspa; a Portage brought them to the
Chavarro which is an eastern tributary of the Rio Caura;
they descended the latter river to the mouth of the Erevato,
and following its course upwards to its sources where there
was an other Portage, they arrived after a three days journey
over Savannahs, at the Rio Manipiare and the Ventuari.
This labyrinth of rivers, thus afforded an inland-communi
cation between the lower Orinoco and its upper banks or
the Paraguá.

The mission of Santa Bárbara consisted during Humboldt’s
visit of 120 .
inhabitants, who manifested considerable
traces of industry. The missionary who resides here,
attends likewise mass in Esmeralda, perhaps five
or six times a year.

Leaving Santa Bárbara; the traveller enjoys a beauti
ful aspect of the Siapo mountains, which at a distance
of eighteen leagues, are visible in a north-western direction;
the vegetation of the banks of the Orinoco is luxuriant and
diversified, and arborescent ferns ,
mix with palms. Having
passed the rivulets Queianuma, Ubua and Masao, we
arrive at the mission of San Fernando de Atabapo. The
situation of this village is near the confluence of the
Orinoco, the Atabapo and the Guaviare. Humboldt found
about 226 .
inhabitants there; they appeared to be more
civilised than the Indians of the other missions; – the
village was surrounded by good pasturage on which
seven or eight cattle were grazing. There were likewise
plantations of Cacao, Cassava and Plantains and
several Pirijao-palms, which gave to the village a very
picturesque appearance. The trunk of the Pirijao
or Pihiguao is about sixty feet high and guarded with
thorns; below its pinnated leaves appears a cluster of fruits,
each two or three inches in diameter, which at first yellow
like an apple, grow purple in proportion as they ripen.
Though the tree bears only three clusters, each consists of
from fifty to eighty fruits, they furnish a farinaceous
substance of colour ressembling that of the yellow of an
egg, slightly saccharine and extremely nutricious, which
when boiled or roasted affords a very wholesome nourish
ment. – The missionary, who resided here had the
title of president of the missions on the Orinoco and
superintended the twenty-six ecclesiastics, settled on the
banks of the Rio Negro, Cassiquiare, Atabapo, Caura and
Orinoco.

Humboldt is of opinion that the Guaviare might
be considered with more right the continuation
of the Orinoco ,
than the Paraguá or that part of the
river which comes from Esmeralda and has been
called by the natives the Paraguá. He adduces for the
correctness of his assertion, that if the river from San
Fernando to its delta, opposite Trinidad, was considered
a continuation of the Guaviare, it would offer through
its whole course a more uniform and natural
direction from south-west to north-east, along
its whole length, from San Fernando de los LlanosVielmehr: San Juan de los Llanos.
and the eastern declivities of the Andes, to its delta;
and he observes further that the general aspect of the river
Guaviare has much more of the character of the Orinoco
below San Fernando, than of the Paraguá above
San Fernando; and that the larger crocodiles and
dolphins, which frequent the lower Orinoco are like
wise to be met with in the Guaviare, while none are
to be found in the Paraguá; – he concludes by observing:
that European Geographers are wrong to deviate from the
opinion of the Indians, who are the best Geographers
of their own country, and who assert that the Paraguá
or upper Orinoco is only a branch of the river and
the Guaviare the continuation of the Orinoco.

Entering the Atabapo, the traveller finds a great change
in the constitution of the atmosphere, the colour of the
stream and the nature of the trees which skirt its
banks. The mosquitoes disappear entirely and instead
of the turbid waters of the Orinoco, loaded with earthy
matter, those of the Atabapo, are though of a dark colour, are|clear are clear
and agreable of taste. – Humboldt followed the course of the
Atabapo in order to reach the Rio Negro and San Carlos
by a shorter route, than that which offers the Cassiquiare.
After having desascended the Atabapo to the mission of San
Balthasar, he entered the Rio Temi and afterwards
the Tuamini; where at the mission San Antonio de
Javita the canoe was carried by land over an isthmus
of 6000 .
toises (= 38.375 .
feet or about seven statute miles and
a half) to the Canno Pimichin, which flows into the Rio Negro. Humboldt makes a comparison between the two routes
according to which by chosing the portage of the Pimichin
the journey to San Carlos may be shortened seven days,
