Where the Orinoco flows from South to north, its shores
are flat and skirted by dense forests. Humboldt found the
strength of its current to be five feet in a second (1 foot
= 12.789 .
inches english). We pass the mouth of the Rio
Mataveni and arrive at the junction of the Rio
Zama. The Rio Vichada is the next river of conse
quence, which flows into the Orinoco. Mess: Messieurs Humboldt
and Bonpland landed at its mouth, to examine the
plants of that neighbourhood. The forests were here
thinner than usual and innumerable small granitic
rocks rose from the plain, presenting the appearance
of prisms, ruined columns and towers from fifteen to
twenty feet in height. If the primitive form of these
rocks did not show the contrary, one might suppose
to be transplanted amidst the rocks of Adersbach
in Bohemia, or of Streitberg, or Fantasie in Franconia.
The rocks there, – (which are of sandstone and lime
stone and of a secondary formation) can not cannot offer
a more picturesque appearance than those at the
Vichada and the illusion of being transplanted
amidst them, might be encreased by observing
the soil and granitic rocks covered with mosses
and liken lichen ressembling the Cladonia pyxidata
of northern Europe. M. Bonpland found at
the Vichada several specimens of the T L aurus
cinnamamoides, a very aromatic species of cinna
mon; known at the missions of the Orinoco by
the name of Varimacu and of Canelilla; this
Species is likewise to be met with in the valley
of the Rio Caura and to the eastward of the great
Cataracts.

The Rio Vichada is next to the Meta and Guaviare, the
largest branch which comes from the west. Since forty
years – (namely in 1800 .
) says Humboldt, it has not been na
vigated by a European; I could not procure myself any
information respecting its sources, but I suppose that they
are like those of the Tomo, in the large plains, south of
Casimena, and that they can not cannot be at a great distance
from those of the Meta. The whole extent of land between
the Meta, Vichada and Guaviare at a distance of four miles
from their banks, and which is supposed to be inhabited
by the Chiricoas, a savage tribe of Indians, is entirely
unexplored by Europeans.

On the eastern side enters the Rio Sipapo or Tipapu.
It was visitted visited by father Gili in 1757 .
and it is thought
that it has its sources in the Cerros de Sipapo; the aspect
of the latter varies every hour of the day. „At sunrise the
dense vegetation“, says HumboldtHumboldt 1814–1829, V, 175. Vgl. Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 381., „with which they are
covered, was tinged with a dark green inclining to brown,
so peculiar to landscapes where trees with thick leaves
prevail; broad and deep shadows were projected over the
neighbouring plain, forming a strong contrast with
the light diffused over the ground, in the air, and upon the
water; but when towards noon, the sun had reached the
zenith, the strong shadows of disappeared vanished and the whole
groupe appeared to be veiled in a vapour, the azure colour
of which was much deeper than that of the lower regions;
– it softened the outlines of the rocks and moderated the
effects of light and gave to the landscape an aspect of calm
ness and repose.“

A perpetual calm seems to reign to the south of the
Cataracts; it is attributed by Humboldt, to the winding
of the rivers, the shelter of the mountains, the dense forest and
frequent rains. Neither on the banks of the Rio Negro and
the Cassiquiare, nor at the foot of the Duida, or in the
mission of Santa Bárbara, the rustling of the leaves, which
at the torrid zone has such a particular charm for
Europeans, interupts the silence, spread over the landscape.

The Island of Piedra Raton attracts next our attention,
it is about three miles and a half long and presents the
surprising aspect of a vegetation in progress; mosses
and likens lichens first settle upon the rocks which on their
decay afford the first vegetable earth; aquatic plants
interwoven with lianas are carried by the current to
its shores and thus accumulate that in a short time
they cover with verdure, the formerly nacked naked rocks.
Humboldt determined the situation of the island,
and found it to be in latitude 5° 4′ 31″ north and in
longtitude longitude 68° 17′ west.

In the vicinity of the mission San José de M
Towards the east in the extreme distance, we discover
the great chain of the Cunevami mountains to rise over
the horizon, ressembling in their structure the Mesa
of the Bergantin in the vicinity of Cumaná; one of
its peaks, the Calitamini, reflects at sunset a reddish glare
of light. No person has approached as yet this mountain,
the height of which Humboldt supposes not to be
above 600 .
toises (= 3835 feet)

We enter now a series of Cataracts which for a
considerable distance obstruct even the boat-navigation
of the Orinoco. The Cataracts (Raudales) of Maypures
and Atures are the most celebrated for extent and
picturesque scenery. The Indians call them Quittuna
and Mappara, but the missionaries denominated them
as mentioned above after the first tribes which they assembl
ed in their vicinity. They are forty-one miles distant from
each other and may be said to divide the christian
establishments of Spanish Guiana into two unequal
parts; those situated between the lower cataract or
that of Atures, being called the missions of the lower Orinoco,
and those between the upper cataract and the mountains
of Duida, the missions of the upper; the lower section
including its sinuosities comprehends 897 .
miles while
that of the upper is 576 .
miles.

In the vicinity of the mission San José de Maypures
is the celebrated cataract called by the Indians Quittuna.
A granitic groupe detaches itself from the mountain
chains of Cunavami and Calitami and extends near
Maypures beyond the western bank of the Orinoco.
From the eastern part of this mountain chain flows
the Sanariapo, from the western the streamlets Cameji
and Taparo. The hills surround the village in a half
circle, through which the river forces its way by
a break at the western end of this majestic amphi
theatre, between the streams Toparo and Sanariapo. The
cataract is partly formed by an archipelago of islands,
filling the bed of the river to the length of 3000 toises
(= 19 188 feet) partly by dikes of granitic rocks which
occasionally join them together. The largest of these dikes
or shelves are in a direction from south to north, the
Purimarimi, the Manimi and the Salto de la
Sardinia, the latter of which is about nine feet high
and forms a beautiful waterfall. To obtain a full view
of these falls, Humboldt ascended the eminence of Manimi
a granitic ridge rising from the savanah, – to the
north of the small church. This hill forms the eastern
limit of a plain that was formerly occupied by the
waters of the river, exhibiting rocks similar to those of
the islands of the cataract.

When one attains the summit of the rock, says Humboldt;
he suddenly sees a sheet of foam, a mile in extent.
Enormous masses of rock, of an iron-blackness, emerge
from its bosom, some of a mammillar form and grouped
like basaltic hills, others ressembling towers, castles and
ruins. Their dark colour contrasts with the silvery
whiteness of the foam. Every rock and islet is covered
with tufts of stately trees, forming groves. From the
base of these prominences, as far as the eye can reach,
there hangs over the river a dense mist, through which
the tops of majestic palms are seen to penetrateDieses Zitat ist eine wörtliche Übernahme aus William MacGillivrays The travels and researches of Alexander von Humboldt (MacGillivray/Humboldt 1832), 251.
Humboldt conjectures that it is the Vadigai Vadgiai -palm,
a new species of Oredoxa, the trunk of which attains
eighty feet. Its pinnated leaves, which stand almost
upright, are covered with a glistening varnish..
At every hour of the day this sheet of foam presents
a different aspect; sometimes the mountains-isles
and palms project their long shadow over it; sometimes
the rays of the setting sun are refracted in the humid
cloudcloud that covers the cataract, when coloured arches
are formed that vanish and re-appear by turns.

Humboldt thinks it possible, to avoid the Cataract
of Maypures and that the delay at present connected
with its passage might be materially lessened, by simply
uniting the two small rivers Cameji and Torparo by a
canal, which at the utmost would not be more than 2850 .
toises (= 18250 feet) in length.

The Raudal de Guahibos offers an other another impeachment
to a free navigation; the traveller is here obliged to leave the
canoe which is drawn over the dike. The river is 5115 .
feet
across and dangerous in consequence of its strong current,
precipitating itself over the dike.Vgl. MacGillivray/Humboldt 1832, 250. MacGillivray gibt die Breite des Orinoko mit 1705 Yards an, die Schomburgk in britische Fuß umrechnet. The Gneissrocks exhibit
circular holes produced by the friction of pebbles; similar
holes are observed at the rapids of Garcita, sometimes at an
elevation of more than 190 feet above the surface of the current;
they must be likewise ascribed to the erosion of the waters
which formerly stood much higher than at present. Opposite
the mouth of the Rio Cataniapo, is the Puerta de arriba
or the place of re-embarkation for travellers, who ascend
the river, coming from the north. Arrived at the lower
falls, they are obliged to leave the canoes, which are unloaded
and drawn over the dikes and rocks by the aid of ropes;
when the torrents happen to be too violent or the bars
too high, the canoes are taken ashore and drawn upon
rollers along the margin of the river until the river
becomes again navigable.

The mission of San Juan Nepomuceno de los
Atures is situated at the distance of a league from the
foot of the great cataract, called by the Indians
Maparrea and is formed like that of Quittuna by innumerable
rocky islets and by compact dikes of granite, which crossing
the river connect two spurs (groupes) of mountains,
that diverge from the Parime range, and run at right
angles to this part of the river. Along a space of
more than five miles, the Orinoco is traversed by
numerous dikes of granitic rock, forming natural
dams (like those of the Dnieper near the village Staroi-
Kaidack) filled with islands of every form, some rocky and
precipitious, whilst other ressemble shoals; by these the
river is broken up into torrents, dashing its spray against
the rocks, which are covered by a dense vegetation of Iaguas
and Cucuritos, with leaves ressembling stately plumes and
a mass of palm-trees raise their pinnated leaves even
above the foam of the river. The Indians of the mission,
which lead the canoe across the Raudal, have given
names to the most remarkable rocks and dikes; thus
we have, commencing from the south, the cascade of
Toucan, the salto del Piapoco, and between the Islands of
Avaguri and Javavireni, the Raudal of the same name.
The Orinoco appears here to be divided in so many arms
or foaming currents, each endeavouring to force a passage
through the rocks; one is astonished to see the small quantity
of water, which is observable, –
the subterranean cascades,
which are formed by the water being ingulfed in caverns, –
and the roar caused by the waves, which rush foaming
against the rocks.

Humboldt says, he was surprised to find, that with
all the whirling and foaming of the waters, the roar of
which may be heard at a distance of more than three
miles, the height of the fall in its whole length does
not exceed 28 twenty-eight feet perpendicular. – When the
rush of the cataract is heard in the plain, that surrounds
the mission of Atures, one fancies to be near a coast
skirted by reefs and breakers. The roar is more than three times
encreased by night, when every other noise is hushed, and
when the air is transparent and of uniform density,
and consequently the slightest sound reaches the ear
without interruption.

The natural scenery around Atures is described as sublime
and most picturesque; lofty mountains that bound the horizon
on every side, contribute to the romantic appearance by their
form and the nature of their vegetation. To the west of Atures;
a pyramidical mountain, the peak of Uniana, rises from a
plain to a height of upwards 3000 feet, and the Savannahs
at its foot present a surprising luxuriance. The state of the
mission itself, was found by Humboldt in most deplorable
circumstances, which he partly ascribed to the general in
salubrity of the climate, bad nourishment and the practice
of preventing pregnancy by the use of deleterious herbs.
The Mosquitos are so tormenting that the inhabitants
of Maypures leave the village at night and sleep at
the little islands in a the midst of cataracts, where these
insects are less numerous. The lower strata of air to the
height of nearly twenty feet from the ground, are sometimes
filled with them, as to give the appearance of a con
tensed condensed vapour. During the day the inhabitants are
harrassed by the mosquitos, which are succeeded at
night by a species of gnats called Zancudos.

Before we leave Atures, we must pay a visit to
the cave of Ataruipe, which is the sepulchre of the Atures,
a tribe now extinct. Humboldt visitted visited the same on
the 31st May 1800. The cave is in the most remote part
of the valley, on the declivity of a steep mountain, shaded
by a thick forest. „We soon“, says heHumboldt 1814–1829, V, 617–618. Vgl. Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 597., „reckoned in this
tomb of a whole extinct nation tribe , near six hundred
skeletons, well preserved and so regularly placed, that
it would have been difficult to make an error in their
number. Every skeleton reposes in a sort of basket,
made of the leave-stalks of the palm-tree; these baskets
which the natives call Mapires, have the form of a squarebag square bag –
their size is according to the age of the dead, from ten inches
to three feet four inches; the skeletons in them being bent
together.“

Where the river meets the Anaveni, which has its
sources at the eastern mountains, the navigation becomes,
comparatively speaking, less obstructed; although there
are rapids in the vicinity of San Borjá and Carichana,
and a series of whirlpools and rapids caused by a chain
of small rocks at the Raudal de Camiseta and the
Boca del Infierno, however they may me be passed without
much danger; a greater danger to the navigation of
the lower Orinoco, arises from natural rafts, consisting
of trees which have been dislodged from its banks and
are interwoven with lianas and covered by aquatic
plants and which are borne away in its current. Destruction
threadens threatens the vessel which should have the misfortune
to strike against one of them during night.

Having passed the island of Panumana, which is
rich in plants, the next object of interest is the mission
of Santa Borja, consisting, at Humboldt’s time, of
six houses inhabited by non-catechised Guahibos,
differing in their manners but little from the savage
tribe of the same name. Above the rapids of Tabajé
to the mouth of the Rio Meta, the Orinoco is free
from shoals and rapids. Next to the Guaviare, this
is the largest river, which enters from the west. The
scenery at the union of these streams offers a very
imposing aspect; solitary peaks of granite rise
on the eastern side, whilst vast sandy shores inter
vene between the banks and the forest. In order
to put a restraint to the Guahiboes, the missionaries
founded at the confluence of the Meta and Orinoco the
Villa de San Carlos, but their plan did not succeed. M.
Roulin
visitted visited the same in March 1824; at a short
distance from San Carlos, a mestizo by the name of
Cyriaco had founded a small village called San Simon.

The Rio Meta flows through the extensive plains
of Casanare and is navigable to the foot of the Andes of
New Grenada. Its mean depth is thirty-six feet and its
maximum eighty-four. It arises from the union of
two rivers, which descend from the Paramos de Chingosa
and from Suma Paz; the first is the Río Negro with
its tributary, the Pachaquiaro, and the second is the
Rio de Aguas blancas or Umadea. Their conjunction
takes place near the Port of Marayal. From Passo
de la Cabulla, where travellers to Bogotá leave the
Río Negro, the distance to that town is about from
thirty-two to forty miles. From the villages of Yiramene
and Cabullaro, to those of Guanapolo and Sta Rosalia
de Cabapuna, a distance of upwards of 240 miles,
the banks of the Meta were in 1800 more thickly
populated, than those of the Orinoco; but from the
mouth of the Río Pauta and that of the Casanare
its shores to a distance of 50 .
miles are infested
by the wild Indians, belonging to the tribe of the
Guahibos, wh ich o often attack travellers. The number
of this tribe is said to amount to several thousand;
they form rafts twelve feet in length and three feet in
width and fasten fifteen or sixteen together bywith the vines
of the Paulinia,
Dolcihos Dolichos , Cissus and other
creepers.

This river would afford the best opportunity to reach Santa
Fé de Bogota from the lower Orinoco, and as its course and
direction appears to be still imperfectly known to
Europeans, and as its geographical situation is of such
importance, – affording the means of a water-communi
cation between the provinces of New Grenada and Guiana;
I feel anxious to leave here the Orinoco and to enter the
Meta for the further continuance of my journey.

Thus I have conducted the reader to the end of my
journey upon one of America’s mightiest rivers and
I would take leave already here, and pursue my solitary
course upon unknown ground, if I did not consider
it my duty to throw firstly a cursory glance at the
continuation of the Orinoco to its Delta.

In the middle of the river and opposite to the
mouth of the Rio Meta, stands a solitary rock,
notorious for the strong current and large whi ch rl pools which
surround it and that have been known to keep
canoes for two days at one and the same place; it
has been called the rock of patience (Piedra de la paciencia).
Humboldt determined here the longtitude longitude of the mouth
of the Rio Meta and found it to be 67° 44′ 14″ west from
Greenwhich. The left bank of the Orinoco from the mission
of Cabruto, to the mouth of the river of Senaruco, a
distance of nearly two degrees of latitude, is entirely
inhabited, but to the westward of the rapids of Carioca,
Don Felix Relinchon has formed a village of Jaruros
and Otomac Indians. – The Raudal de Cariven con
sists of a number of granitic rocks, which to a distance
of 640 .
fathoms fill the bed of the river; the channels
between them are often very narrow, affording scarcely
sufficient place for the canoe to pass. Near the Piedra
del Tigre, a large rock, the depth of the Orinoco was found by
Humboldt so great, that with a sounding-line of 22 .
french
ells (1 ell = 54 .
inches english = 99 .
feet?) no bottom could be
found reached.Schomburgks Umrechnung ist nicht schlüssig. Humboldt gibt 22 brasses an, die Williams in ihrer Übersetzung in 22 Fathoms (1 Fathom = 72 Inches) überträgt. MacGillivray rechnet Humboldts Angabe in 140 britische Fuß um. Vgl. Humboldt 1814–1825, II, 282; Humboldt 1814–1829, V, 827; MacGillivray/Humboldt 1832, 235. In a bay between two promontories of
granite, there is the port of Carichana, from whence the
mission of that name, is three miles in-land. The Orinoco
is here somewhat narrower, but widens again at the
mouth of the Río Paruasi, where several small islands
and rocks form the little rapids or „los remolinos“.
Near the island of Pararuma famed for turtle-fishery,
the river divides in several branches; their total breadth
has been estimated to be from 2630 .
f to
3200 fathoms; the
shore becomes hereafter precipitous and sinnuous sinuous and
at the Baraguan the river is hemmed in by precipices
of granite, forming part of a groupe of mountains,
through which it has forced its passage by a break; it
is here contracted for some distance to 947 .
fathoms,
whilst its general breadth from the mission of Uruana
opposite the mouth of the Arauca (7° 8′ N. North ) to its confluence
with the Rio Meta (about 6° 20′ N. North ) is from 1600 .
to 2660 .
fathoms. The force of its current is 3.6 .
feet in a second.

The mission of Uruana was founded in 1748 .
by the
Jesuits, it consisted according to Humboldt of 500 .
in
habitants. This traveller measured here the breadth of
the Orinoco, which he found to be 2848 .
fathoms,
at a distance of upwards 582 geographical miles from
its mouth. The Indians of this mission who are
Ottomacs, are known to swallow quantities of earth
for the purpose of satisfying their hunger. When the
waters are low they live of fish and turtles, but when
the rivers swell and they can not cannot procure such food and
much to indolent to raise provisions, they rather prefere prefer
to eat large portions of earth; Humboldt found in their
huts ,
heaps of it, from three to four feet high and piled
up in the form of pyramids. At some distance from
Uruana (about 25 .
miles) is the Playa de la Tortuga
(Turtle-shore) an island celebrated for turtle-fishery and
the quantity of eggs, which a tortoise, the arrau or tortugas
deposits upon its shores during the month of March,
when different tribes of Indians assemble in order to
collect them. The missionaries of Uruana claim the
authority over this I i sland, and one is generally present
to divide the egg-ground into different portions and
to chose a person, who invested with authority to
keep the encampments in order.

Between the Punta Curiquima and the mouth
of the Apure, the Orinoco has been ascertained to
be 2030 .
fathoms wide; during the rainy season it
extends to 5880 .
fathoms (up a w ards of five miles and
and a half. In its vicinity is the mission of San Luis del
Encaramada, formed in 1749 .
by father Gili, the author
of „Storia dell Orinoco“Der erste Band von Filippo Salvadore Gilijs Werk Saggio di storia americana trägt den Titel „Della storia geografica, e naturale, della provincia dell'Orinoco“.. Above the villa Cuycara, near
the village Alta Gracia, turns the river suddenly from
north to east; on its left banks extend the plains of
Venezuela beyond the visible horizon; the right shore
is skirted by impenetrable wood. The population
becomes here more numerous and consists almost
excusively exclusively of whites, mulattos mulattoes and negros negroes ; the
Indians have retired to the interior. After the
embouchure of the Rio Caura has been past,
a long and narrow island divides its bed in two arms;

The Rio Arui is the last river of consequence, which joins the
Orinoco, several other rivers emptie empty themselves into the Orinoco before the traveller reaches Angostura,
but they are of no great importance, none of which I shall
therefore cite. The strength of the current, which near Alta
Gracia amounts to 3.9 .
feet, is between Muritaco and
Bourbon only 2.9 .
feet.

Angostura or Santo Thomé del Angostura has
received its name from being build built on a narrow part
of the river; it stands at the foot of a hill of hornblende-
slate (schiste amphibolique) destitute of all vegetation.
Humboldt determined its situation and found the
cathedral to be in latitude 8° 8′ 11″ north and in longtitude longitude
63° 55′ 6″ west from Greenwhich. It was formerly the capital
of Spanish Guiana and has been famed at later times
for the congress which was held here on the 15th February
1819. This congress eventually proposed and effected the
union of New Granada and Venezuela & Guiana into one Government
under the name of Colombia, by the fundamental law of the
republic, dated 17th December 1819.

The width of the river between the two forts of San
Gabriel and San Rafael is 604½ fathoms. From Angostura
to the The delta and its principal mouth, the Boca de Navios,
is 3° 52′ E. East from Angostura; the principal rivers which
enter from the south, are the Carony, Imataca and
Aoguire. The Carony joins the Orinoco in about 62° 42′
western longtitude longitude ; it is navigable from the Villa de
Barcelloneta to the village Guri. The great Salto
celebrated for its picturesque scenery, is somewhere higher
up than the village Aguacagua or Carony; the height
of this cascade is estimated from 15 .
to 20 .
feet.

In the vicinity of la Vieja Guiana, the river is filled with rocky
islands; its width amounts here to 692 .
fathoms (Humboldt
vol volume 4Vielmehr Humboldt 1814–1829, Vol. V, 757..
Chap. Chapter XXIV .
); the city which was formerly the capital of Spanish
Guiana, has been destroyed, but the fortifications were stillhave remained
visible. Six leagues below Guiana, the Orinoco sends an arm
(the Canno Manamo) to the Bocas chicas; here stands the village San Rafael; below
the same, near the villages Imataca and Zacupana,
25 .
leagues from the Punta Barima, divides the Orinoco
in two branches, named like the above two villages; they
remain separated for a distance of upwards of fourteen
leagues; after their junction the bed of the Orinoco widens
to 3195 .
fathoms (upwards of three nautical miles).
It flows finally into the Atlantic by about fifty mouths,
seven of which are navigable. The principal mouth,
the Boca de Navíos, is south-east from Trinidad; its
width has been differently stated. The island of Cangrejos
is situated therein and separated from the alluvial
soil to the northward by a small Canal, calledand extends between the
Boca de Nuina, between which and the Boca de Mariusas
(i.e. the alluvial soil) in such a manner, that the result
of a measurement may amount to fourteen or
twenty leagues, according to the manner in which it
has been executed, whether from Punta Barima to
the nearest land, in a direction contrary to the current,
or from the same Cap to the eastern point of isla
Cangrejos. The navigable channel is partly obstructed
by a bar with only 18 feet water; its width has been
stated to be from 2660 .
to 2980 .
fathoms. As soon
as Punta Barima has been doubled, the real bed of
the river is only 3195 .
feet wide.

The head of the tide is during the month of
April, beyond Angostura, at a distance of eighty-five
leagues from its mouth. At the conjunction with the
Carony, the water rises 1 .
foot 3 .
inches; at Punta
Barima from 2 .
to 3 .
feet. The greatest distance between
the mouths of the Orinoco, amounts to forty-seven
leagues, namely between Punta Barima and the
most western of the Bocas chicas. Its descent from
the Rio Apure to the Boca de Navios, a distance of a
thousand nautical miles amounts only to three
inches and a fourth on each nautical mile. If we
suppose its sources to be 30 .
leagues to the eastward of
Esmeralda, the length of its course (including its sinuosities)
above Maypures will amount to 220 .
leagues and from
thence to its mouth 299 .
leagues.

At the time that its sources were thought to be
at the foot of the Andes, its periodical|innundations periodical innundations
were ascribed to the melting of the snow, but since we
know the contrary and similar phenomena have been
observed with respect to other rivers in the equinoctial
regions, it must be attributed to the rains, which commence
to fall after the vernal equinox. It begins to rise after
the 25th of March with about an inch in twenty-four
hours; sometimes it falls a few inches in April. It
rises until the month of July, when it reaches its
highest and remains then stationary until the
25th of August, when it falls gradually in the same
manner as it rose and is lowest in January and
February.

The perpendicular rise of the lower Orinoco
is considered to be sixteen fathoms, according to others
only thirteen fathoms. In the vicinity of Carichana
Humboldt observed the marks of the late innundations
eight fathoms above the level of the current, but at various
places, black bands and erosions showed him that once the
river must have stood 107 .
to 138 feet
higher above the
present highest water-mark . At every flood it overspreads
a vast country, from 80 to 90 .
miles each side, pre
senting to the eye a boundless expanse of water.

We have now traced the course of the Orinoco from the
Raudal de Guaharibos, the extent of our present knowledge
of its course, to its termination opposite Trinidad; we
have seen that the river at the upper part is known
to the natives by as the
Paraguá; it has been shown
that in its course it describes almost three fourth of
an ellipsis, the large axis of which has the direction of
a parallel. Having left the Alpine valleys of Maraguaca,
it takes a western direction, and having given an
an arm to the Rio Negro, it flows northwest, when,
after having effected the union with the Guaviare,
it turns suddenly towards the north, and flows in
the direction of a meridian to the embouchure of
the Apure; here it changes for a second time its
direction (point de rebroussement) and instead
of continuing its course from south to north, it
turns from West to east and after a course of
upwards 1500 .
miles, poures pours its waters into the
Atlantic at a direct distance of not more than
250 .
miles from its sources. Finally it is a river
whose Sources are situated within two degrees of
its mouth and which offers three peculiarities,

of land, which Geographers would consider

and Amazon

secondly, its bifurcation, by which it gives a

thirdly, its adherence to the mountains of
Parime
